title: Native shell, shared contracts
summary: Keep platform calls behind one adapter, protect credentials and deep links, and resolve cross-device sync conflicts by revision.

scenario.briefing: The same web bundle now ships to browsers and to iOS and Android through Capacitor. A synced web directory is not a store build: the native project still needs signing, icons, permission descriptions, and versioning. The shell stores the session token in Preferences, opens any incoming URL, and lets the last device win every sync. Move platform calls behind one adapter and keep the shared contract intact.

misconceptions.description: Using Preferences as an encrypted credential store.
misconceptions.testDescription: Native credentials use secure storage and web sessions use a server-set cookie.
misconceptions.feedback: Preferences is plain storage. Use the platform Keychain or Keystore for credentials.

misconceptions.description: Routing a deep link without validating its host and session.
misconceptions.feedback: Any app can send a custom-scheme link. Restrict hosts, validate the route, and require an authenticated session.

misconceptions.description: Overwriting a newer server revision during sync.
misconceptions.testDescription: Sync keeps the newer server revision and reports a conflict.
misconceptions.feedback: Last-write-wins silently discards another device's edit. Compare revisions and surface a conflict.

sections.title: A synced web directory is not a store build
sections.body: npx cap sync copies the web bundle and updates native dependencies. It does not sign the app, set the bundle version, add required permission descriptions, produce icons, or upload a reviewable binary. The Xcode workspace and Android project still go through their own build and release steps.

sections.title: One adapter, two implementations
sections.body: Shared screens call an interface. Native code uses Keychain or Keystore, app URL events, and local notifications; web code uses httpOnly cookies, the History API, and the Notifications API. Platform checks stay in the adapter, not in every component. Preferences and localStorage are plain storage, so credentials belong in a secure storage plugin backed by iOS Keychain or Android Keystore.

sections.title: Deep links cross a trust boundary
sections.body: Parse the URL, check the scheme and host against an allowlist, restore the session, then route. A link that lands on an authenticated screen before authorization is a bypass.

sections.title: Sync needs a revision
sections.body: Each write carries the revision it was based on. If the server revision is newer, keep the server value or ask for a merge. Last-write-wins silently destroys another device's work.

sections.title: Ask for notification permission in context
sections.body: Request permission when the user turns on alerts and handle denial. A launch-time prompt is usually denied and cannot be shown again on iOS.

vocabulary.definition: A native runtime that loads a web bundle inside an iOS or Android shell and exposes platform APIs through plugins.
One interface that shared code calls, with native and web implementations behind it.
A URL that opens a specific screen in the app, often from another app or a browser.
A monotonically increasing version number attached to a record so concurrent writes can be ordered.
Platform-backed storage such as iOS Keychain or Android Keystore that is not readable as plain files.

steps.title: Adapt the shell without leaking platform details
steps.prompt: Edit native.ts. Put secure storage, notification permission, and deep link handling behind one adapter. Reject links from other hosts or without a session, and merge synced orders by revision instead of overwriting newer server state.

tests.description: Native credentials use secure storage and web sessions use a server-set cookie.
Deep links are limited to an allowed host and require a session.
Notification permission is checked before it is requested.
Sync keeps the newer server revision and reports a conflict.
includes: throw new Error("Sync conflict: pull the newer server record first")
return { saveSession, readSession, clearSession, requestNotifications, onDeepLink }

hints: Keep native credentials in Keychain or Keystore.
Treat deep links as untrusted input.
Check notification permission before requesting it.
Resolve sync conflicts by revision and report them instead of overwriting.

artifact.title: native.ts
artifact.caption: Tokens go to localStorage, deep links route without an authorization check, and order writes always replace the server record.

findings.label: The access token is written to localStorage.
The deep link handler navigates without checking a session or an allowed host.
The order write always replaces the server record, even when the server revision is newer.
The artifact stores the token in the platform keychain.
The artifact compares revisions before writing.

verdicts.label: Block the change until credentials, routing, and sync are fixed.
Ship it; the behavior is acceptable for a first release.
Only naming and formatting need work.

steps.explanation: localStorage exposes the token to any script on the origin. The deep link handler routes any URL before checking a session or host. The order write carries no revision, so a newer server record is overwritten. The artifact does not use the platform keychain and never compares revisions.
hints: Find credentials stored where page script can read them.
Check the deep-link allowlist and session requirement.
Ask what happens when two devices edit the same record.
Block the change: tokens in localStorage, an open deep link, and last-write-wins lose data.
